A temperate-climate guide. Shift by your last frost date.

  • 6 weeks before last frost

  • 4 weeks before

    Start broccoli, cabbage, and lettuce indoors. Harden off on nice days.

  • 2 weeks before

  • 2 weeks after

  • Midsummer

    Side-dress with compost. Water in the morning. Watch for pests.

  • First frost

    Harvest everything tender. Plant garlic for next year. Cover hardy greens.

Your local extension office has a free planting calendar by zip code.

A predictable rhythm for a happy starter. Adjust to your kitchen temperature.

Sourdough Starter Feeding Timeline

A steady rhythm keeps your starter bubbly and ready. Here's a typical 12-hour feeding cycle.

  • Day 0 · 8:00 AM

    Feed: 1 part starter, 1 part flour, 1 part water. Stir well, cover loosely.

  • Day 0 · 8:00 PM

    Check for rise. If doubled, feed again. If not, wait 2–4 more hours.

  • Day 1 · 8:00 AM

    Feed again. Starter should smell yeasty and tangy, not like acetone.

  • Day 1 · 8:00 PM

    Second daily feed. Keep it warm (75–80°F). Cold slows everything down.

  • Day 2 · 8:00 AM

    Feed. Watch for predictable doubling within 4–6 hours of each feed.

  • Day 2 · 3:00 PM

    Peak activity: use it now for baking, or feed and refrigerate.

  • Day 3 · 8:00 AM

    If refrigerated, take out, feed, and let it warm up before using.

Bubbles, rise, and a pleasant sour smell mean it's happy. If liquid forms on top (hooch), pour it off and feed.

Knife Sharpening Timeline

A sharp knife is a safe knife. Here's the process.

  1. Gather: Whetstone (1000/6000 grit), honing rod, towel.
  2. Soak: Soak the stone in water for 10–15 minutes.
  3. Angle: Hold knife at 15–20 degrees. Maintain that angle.
  4. Sweep: Push the blade across the stone in sweeping motions. 10 passes per side.
  5. Flip: Repeat on the other side.
  6. Hone: Use the honing rod to realign the edge.
  7. Test: Slice a tomato or paper. It should glide.
Don't skip the honing—it keeps the edge true between sharpenings.

Sewing a Button Timeline

Lost a button? Here's how to put it back.

  1. Thread: Cut 18" of thread, knot the end, thread the needle.
  2. Anchor: Push needle from back to front where the button goes.
  3. Position: Place button on needle, then push needle back down through another hole.
  4. Repeat: Go through each pair of holes 3–4 times.
  5. Shank: Before final pass, wrap thread around the stitches under the button to create a shank.
  6. Secure: Knot on the back and trim.
A shank gives room for thick fabric and keeps the button from pulling tight.

Turkey Roast Timeline

Hi user_name — a 12–14 lb bird, unstuffed. Times shift if yours is bigger.

  • 3 days out

    Move turkey from freezer to fridge

    Why

    Fridge thaw is about 24 hours per 4–5 lb. Rushing it in water risks uneven thawing.

  • 1 day out

    Dry brine: salt all over, uncovered in the fridge

    Why

    Dry air firms the skin; salt seasons deep. Uncovered is the point.

  • 3.5 hrs before

    Pull from fridge, pat dry, let it sit at room temp 45 min

    Why

    A cold center cooks slower and dries the outside before the middle is done.

  • 3 hrs before

    Oven to 425°F, bird on a rack in a pan

    Why

    High heat first crisps skin; a rack keeps the bottom from steaming.

  • 30 min in

    Drop to 325°F, tent breast loosely with foil

    Why

    Breast meat hits target before thighs do. Foil slows the breast down.

  • 2 hrs in

    Check temp: 155°F breast, 175°F thigh

    Why

    Carryover heat adds 5–10°F while it rests. Pull early, not late.

  • 15 min out

    Remove foil, crank to 500°F for browning

    Why

    Watch it — this stage goes from golden to burnt in about three minutes.

  • Done

    Rest 30 min, loosely tented, before carving

    Why

    Resting lets juices redistribute. Carve early and they end up on the board.

If the breast hits 155 before the thigh is ready, tent the whole bird and give it 15 more minutes. The thigh is the one that forgives.

    Wash your hair, skip the heavy product

    Why

    Stylists can read clean, product-free hair. A waxy buildup hides your actual texture.

  • Morning of

    Bring one photo and one sentence

    Why

    Photos carry more than words. One sentence — length, shape, or "same but shorter" — fills in the rest.

  • Arrive

    Five minutes early, coat off, phone away

    Why

    Being ready when the chair opens keeps the whole shop on schedule.

  • First 10 min

    Consultation: say what you hated about the last cut

    Why

    Stylists learn more from what went wrong than from what you want. Be specific and kind.

  • Next 30 min

    The cut. If it's going wrong, say so early

    Why

    A trim is easy to correct. Waiting until the end means losing length you wanted to keep.

  • Last 10 min

    Style and dry. Watch how they do it

    Why

    The product and motion they use at home is the difference between the mirror and tomorrow morning.

  • Before you pay

    Ask about rebooking, tip, book it

    Why

    You're already here and they know your hair now. Rebooking takes ten seconds and saves a phone call later.

If you liked the cut, ask for the same stylist by name next time. Consistency beats luck.

Board Game Night Timeline

Hey user_name — four players, one medium-weight game, about three hours.

  • 2 days out

    Pick the game and send a how-to-play video link

    Why

    Watching a ten-minute video beforehand turns a 30-minute teach into a five-minute refresher.

  • Day of, 6:00 PM

    Clear the table, good lighting, chairs that don't wobble

    Why

    Nobody can reach the far side of a cluttered table, and dim light means misread cards.

  • 6:30

    Snacks that don't grease fingers; drinks on coasters off the table

    Why

    Chips and cards do not mix. Napkins and a side table solve most of it.

  • 7:00

    People arrive. Ten minutes of catching up, then sit

    Why

    Letting the chat happen before the rules means fewer interruptions once you start.

  • 7:10

    Teach in this order: goal, turn structure, then the one tricky rule

    Why

    People remember the goal and the flow. Edge cases only stick once they've played a turn.

  • 7:30

    Play a practice round open-handed, no hidden info

    Why

    One open round answers more questions than ten minutes of explaining.

  • 7:45

    Real game. Deal, then let it run

    Why

    Rules questions during play get answered in one sentence. Resist the urge to re-teach.

  • 9:30

    Last round called. Winner announced, table cleared

    Why

    A stated ending keeps the night fun instead of grinding to a halt.

House rule: whoever teaches the game goes last on the first turn. It's the small tax for talking so much.
